United States District Court, [Sample Jurisdiction]

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION FOR APPOINTED COUNSEL
(SAMPLE excerpt for citation verification only. Not legal advice. Not a court filing.)

I. The Sixth Amendment requires appointed counsel in this prosecution.

The right to counsel in a capital case tried in a state court was recognized long before the modern incorporation cases. Powell v. Alabama, 287 U.S. 45 (1932). Federal felony defendants had a corresponding appointed-counsel rule. Johnson v. Zerbst, 304 U.S. 458 (1938). The Court later declined, for a time, to require appointed counsel in every serious state prosecution. Betts v. Brady, 316 U.S. 455 (1942).

That special-circumstances approach was overruled. The Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and applicable to the States. Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963). The right extends to misdemeanor prosecutions that result in actual imprisonment. Argersinger v. Hamlin, 407 U.S. 25 (1972). Ineffective assistance is measured against an objective standard of reasonableness and prejudice. Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668 (1984).

Appointment of counsel in federal criminal cases is also addressed by statute. 18 U.S.C. § 3006A. The procedural counterpart is Fed. R. Crim. P. 44. The constitutional text is U.S. Const. amend. VI.
